'''''Impatiens glandulifera''''', '''Himalayan balsam''', is a large [[annual plant]] native to the [[Himalayas]].<ref>Webb, D.A., Parnell, J. and Doogue, D. 1996. ''An Irish Flora''. Dundalgan Press (W.Tempest) Ltd. Dundalk</ref> Via human introduction it is now present across much of the Northern Hemisphere and is considered an [[invasive species]] in many areas. Uprooting or cutting the plants is an effective means of control.

In Europe, Himalayan balsam has been included since 2017 in the [[list of invasive alien species of Union concern]] (the Union list).<ref>{{Cite web|title=List of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern – Environment – European Commission|url=https://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/invasivealien/list/index_en.htm|access-date=2021-07-27|publisher=European Commission}}</ref> This implies that the species cannot be imported, cultivated, transported, commercialized, planted, or intentionally released into the environment in the whole of the [[European Union]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=REGULATION (EU) No 1143/2014 of the European parliament and of the council of 22 October 2014 on the prevention and management of the introduction and spread of invasive alien species|url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32014R1143&from=EN}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The common names '''Himalayan balsam''' and '''kiss-me-on-the-mountain''' refer to the plant's native Himalayan mountains.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Himalayan balsam {{!}} The Wildlife Trusts|url=https://www.wildlifetrusts.org/wildlife-explorer/wildflowers/himalayan-balsam|access-date=2020-09-09|website=wildlifetrusts.org}}</ref> '''Ornamental jewelweed''' refers to its cultivation as an ornamental plant.

The [[specific epithet]] ''glandulifera'' is a compound word from ''glándula'' meaning 'small gland', and ''ferre'' meaning 'to bear'.

==Description==
[[File:Impatiens glandulifera.ogg|thumb|Scattering its seeds]]
[[File:Impatiens Glandulifera, leaves.jpg|thumb]]
[[File:Springkraut fg04.jpg|thumb|Glands]]
It typically grows to {{convert|1|to|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} high, with a soft green or red-tinged stem, and lanceolate [[leaf|leaves]] {{convert|5|to|23|cm|in|abbr=on}} long. The crushed foliage has a strong musty smell. Below the leaf stems the plant has [[gland (botany)|glands]] that produce a sticky, sweet-smelling, and edible nectar. The [[flower]]s are pink, with a hooded shape, 3 to 4 cm ({{frac|1|1|4}} to {{frac|1|1|2}} in) tall and 2 cm ({{frac|3|4}} in) broad; the flower shape has been compared to a [[custodian helmet|policeman's helmet]].

After flowering between June and October, the plant forms seed pods 2 to 3 cm ({{frac|3|4}} to {{frac|1|1|4}} in) long and 8 mm broad ({{frac|1|4}} in), which [[Explosive dehiscence|explode]] when disturbed,<ref>Scott, R. 2004. ''Wild Belfast on safari in the city.'' Blackstaff Press. {{ISBN|0 85640 762 3}}</ref> scattering the [[seed]]s up to {{convert|7|m|ft|abbr=off}}.

The green seed pods, seeds, young leaves and shoots are all [[edible]]. The flowers can be turned into a [[Fruit preserves|jam]] or [[parfait]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Gastronomie: Springkraut & Co.: Kräuterkoch Peter Becker macht aus Neophyten Salat|url = https://www.badische-zeitung.de/gastronomie-1/kraeuterkoch-peter-becker-macht-aus-neophyten-salat--49463213.html|access-date = 21 May 2015|date = 13 September 2011|website = Badische Zeitung}}</ref>

The plant was rated in first place for per day nectar production per flower in a [[UK]] plants survey conducted by the AgriLand project which is supported by the UK Insect Pollinators Initiative. However, when number of flowers per floral unit, flower abundance, and [[phenology]] were taken into account, it dropped out of the top ten for most nectar per unit cover per year, as did all plants that placed in the top ten for per-day nectar production per flower, with the exception of common [[comfrey]] (''[[Symphytum officinale]]).''<ref name=Pollinators>{{cite web |title=Which flowers are the best source of nectar? |publisher=Conservation Grade |url=http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ |access-date=2017-10-18 |date=2014-10-15 |archive-date=14 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191214024659/http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Himalayan balsam is native to the Himalayas, specifically to the areas between [[Kashmir]] and [[Uttarakhand]]. In its native range it is usually found at altitudes between 2000 and 2500 m above sea level, although it has been reported at up to 4000 m above sea level.<ref name="BeerlingPerrins">{{cite journal |last1=Beerling |first1=David J. |last2=Perrins |first2=James M. |title=Impatiens Glandulifera Royle (Impatiens Roylei Walp.) |journal=The Journal of Ecology |date=June 1993 |volume=81 |issue=2 |pages=367–382 |doi=10.2307/2261507|jstor=2261507 |bibcode=1993JEcol..81..367B }}</ref>

In Europe the plant was first introduced into the [[United Kingdom]] by [[John Forbes Royle]], professor of medicine at [[King's College, London]] who became Superintendent of the Botanic Gardens, Saharanpur, India.<ref>Valerie Porter, "The Second Field Book of Country Queries" p. 93</ref> It has now become naturalized and widespread across riverbanks.<ref name="BeerlingPerrins" /> At present it can be found almost everywhere across the continent.<ref name="PyšekPrach">{{cite journal |last1=Pyšek |first1=Petr |last2=Prach |first2=Karel |title=Invasion dynamics of Impatiens glandulifera – A century of spreading reconstructed |journal=Biological Conservation |date=1995 |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=41–48 |doi=10.1016/0006-3207(95)00013-T|bibcode=1995BCons..74...41P }}</ref><ref>Scannell, M.J.P. and Synnott, D.M. 1972. ''Census Catalogue of the Flora of Ireland.'' Dublin. Published by the Stationery Office.</ref><ref>Hackney, P. (Ed)1992. ''Stewart & Corry's Flora of the North-East of Ireland.'' The Institute of Irish Studies, The Queen's University of Belfast. {{ISBN|0 85389 446 9}}</ref>

In North America it has been found in the Canadian provinces of [[British Columbia]], [[Manitoba]], [[Ontario]], [[Quebec]], [[Nova Scotia]], [[New Brunswick]], [[Prince Edward Island]] and [[Newfoundland]].<ref name="CanJPlSci">{{cite journal |last1=Clements |first1=David R |last2=Feenstra |first2=Kathleen R |last3=Jones |first3=Karen |last4=Staniforth |first4=Richard |title=The biology of invasive alien plants in Canada. 9. Impatiens glandulifera Royle |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |date=April 2008 |volume=88 |issue=2 |pages=403–417 |doi=10.4141/CJPS06040|doi-access= }}</ref> In the United States it is found on both the east and west coast, seemingly restricted to northern latitudes.<ref name="EDDmaps">{{cite web |title=Himalayan balsam, Impatiens glandulifera Geraniales: Balsaminaceae |url=https://www.eddmaps.org/Species/subject.cfm?sub=12794 |website=EDDMapS.org |access-date=20 November 2018 |language=en}}</ref>

In [[New Zealand]] it is sometimes found growing wild along riverbanks and wetlands.<ref name="NZPCN">{{cite web |title=Impatiens glandulifera |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=4100 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=20 November 2018}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
Himalayan balsam is sometimes cultivated for its flowers. It is now widely established in other parts of the world (such as the British Isles and North America), in some cases becoming a [[weed]]. Its aggressive seed dispersal, coupled with high nectar production which attracts pollinators, often allows it to out-compete native plants. Himalayan balsam also promotes river bank erosion due to the plant dying back over winter, leaving the bank unprotected from flooding.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Greenwood |first1=Phillip |last2=Fister |first2=Wolfgang|last3=Kuhn|first3=Nikolas |title=The potential influence of the invasive plant, Impatiens glandulifera (Himalayan Balsam), on the ecohydromorphic functioning of inland river systems |url=https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU2014/EGU2014-2698.pdf |journal=Geophysical Research Abstracts |pages=2698 |date=2014 |access-date=14 May 2015|bibcode=2014EGUGA..16.2698P }}</ref> Invasive Himalayan balsam can also adversely affect indigenous species by attracting pollinators (e.g. insects) at the expense of indigenous species.<ref>{{cite journal |last2= Brys|first2= Rein|last3= Verboven|first3= Hans A. F.|last4= Hermy|first4= Martin|title=The influence of an invasive plant species on the pollination success and reproductive output of three riparian plant species |journal=Biological Invasions |volume=14 |issue=2 |date=30 July 2011 |doi=10.1007/s10530-011-0067-y |pages=355–365|last1= Thijs|first1= Koen W.|s2cid= 14186232|url= https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/71b3dc7f4f180ee892dcd2a419760aeeef6ce9b5}}</ref> It is considered a "prohibited noxious weed" under the ''Alberta Weed Control Act 2010''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.edmonton.ca/documents/PDF/Weed_Identification_Book.pdf|title=Identification Guide for Alberta Invasive Plants|year=2017 |publisher=[[Wheatland County, Alberta]] |access-date=28 July 2018}}</ref>

In the UK, the plant was first introduced in 1839, at the same time as [[giant hogweed]] and [[Japanese knotweed]].<ref name="Mabey">{{cite episode |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b012qnl4#synopsis |series=Mabey in the wild |title=Indian Balsam |last=Mabey |first=Richard |air-date=25 July 2011 |publisher=BBC |access-date=24 July 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.open.edu/openlearn/nature-environment/natural-history/wanted-himalayan-balsam |title=Wanted!: Himalayan Balsam |work=British Isles: A Natural History |publisher=The Open University |access-date=4 December 2009 }}</ref> These plants were all promoted at the time as having the virtues of "herculean proportions" and "splendid invasiveness" which meant that ordinary people could buy them for the cost of a packet of seeds to rival the expensive orchids grown in the greenhouses of the rich. Within ten years, however, Himalayan balsam had escaped from the confines of cultivation and begun to spread along the river systems of England.<ref name="Mabey"/>

It has now spread across most of the UK, and some local wildlife trusts organise "balsam bashing" events to help control the plant.<ref name="Mabey"/> However, a study by Hejda and Pyšek (2006) concluded that, in some circumstances, such efforts may cause more harm than good. Destroying [[riparian]] stands of Himalayan balsam can open up the habitat for more aggressive [[invasive plant]]s such as [[Japanese knotweed]] and aid in seed dispersal by dropped seeds sticking to shoes. Riparian habitat is suboptimal for ''I. glandulifera'', and spring or autumn flooding destroys seeds and plants. The research suggests that the best way to control the spread of riparian Himalayan balsam is to decrease [[eutrophication]], thereby permitting the better-adapted local vegetation, that gets outgrown by the balsam on watercourses with high nutrient load, to rebound naturally. The researchers caution that their conclusions probably do not hold true for stands of the plant at forest edges and meadow habitats, where manual destruction is still the best approach.

In August 2014, [[CABI (organisation)|CABI]] released a [[rust (fungus)|rust fungus]] in Berkshire, Cornwall and Middlesex in the United Kingdom as part of field trials into the biological control of Himalayan balsam.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cabi.org/news-article/cabi-releases-rust-fungus-to-control-invasive-weed-himalayan-balsam/|title=CABI releases rust fungus to control invasive weed, Himalayan balsam |date=26 August 2014 |website=cabi.org |publisher=CABI |access-date=17 May 2015}}</ref>

Some research also suggests that ''I. glandulifera'' may exhibit [[allelopathy]], which means that it excretes toxins that negatively affect neighboring plants, thus increasing its competitive advantage.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aka.fi/Tiedostot/Viksu/2012ty%C3%B6t/Sofia%20Mononen%20kilpailuty%C3%B6.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=31 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140531185139/http://www.aka.fi/Tiedostot/Viksu/2012ty%C3%B6t/Sofia%20Mononen%20kilpailuty%C3%B6.pdf |archive-date=31 May 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The [[Royal Horticultural Society]] and the [[Centre for Ecology and Hydrology]] recommend that pulling and cutting is the main method of non-chemical control, and usually the most appropriate.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://rhs.org.uk/advice/profile?pid=480 |title=Himalayan Balsam |publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society]] |access-date=2 June 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ceh.ac.uk/sci_programmes/documents/himalayanbalsam.pdf |title=Information Sheet 3: Himalayan Balsam |publisher=[[Centre for Ecology and Hydrology: Centre for Aquatic Plant Management]] |access-date=2 June 2014 |date=2013-03-08 |archive-date=7 February 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140207224532/http://www.ceh.ac.uk/sci_programmes/documents/himalayanbalsam.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Natural Resources Wales]] has used manual methods, such as pulling plants and using [[string trimmer|strimmers]], to largely eradicate Himalayan balsam from reaches of the [[River Ystwyth]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Cyfoeth Issue 3 September 2013|url=http://naturalresources.wales/media/1156/cyfoeth-no3-september-2013.pdf|publisher=Natural Resources Wales|access-date=12 June 2015|page=6}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Uses==
Himalayan Balsam is edible, but should be eaten in moderation as it contains [[oxalates]]<ref>{{cite web | title=Invasive edibles: Himalayan Balsam (Impatiens glandulifera) | date=August 2021 | url=https://www.foragingcoursecompany.co.uk/post/articles-invasive-edibles-himalayan-balsam#: }}</ref>
